title: The Simca P60 Rush engine: what really changes after the Flash
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: When the P60 moves from Flash to Rush, Simca is trying to prolong the Aronde career through mechanical touches as much as through style. For today’s enthusiast, that nuance matters both in buying and in maintenance.
content:
The Rush name can suggest a deep rupture. In reality, it is better read as another step in the way Simca tries to keep the Aronde up to the level of a market that is changing quickly.

From Flash to Rush, more continuity than erasure

The Flash engine had already given the Aronde 1300 a more convincing base than the earliest cars. With the Rush, Simca does not erase that history. The marque rather tries to keep it going through a mechanical tone that feels more current.

That continuity matters for understanding the P60. The model remains a prolongation, even when it presents itself as a new decade’s car.

What this changes in use

For the period driver, the main point lies in flexibility, the sense of modernity and the feeling that the car is not already outdated as competition renews itself strongly.

For today’s collector, it mostly changes the reading of the version and some choices in parts, settings and documentation.

The engine must still be read inside the whole car

As often happens, the engine does not tell everything. An interesting P60 does not reduce itself to its block. It is also judged through version, equipment coherence, body condition and the quality of older repairs.

The Rush therefore matters, but as one clue among others. It helps place the car in the final phase of Aronde history.

This note extends the page the Simca P60. Within the same cluster, the next useful step is How to recognise a Simca P60: what the front end and line change in 1959.
